title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation, not a model error. A synthetic video presented a well-known financial figure as endorsing an investment with claimed large returns, and the victim treated the endorsement as real. The falsehood was carried by the likeness itself, which is why the usual checks on a claim's content would not have helped.

The AI element sat at the front of the fraud, at the point where trust is established, and not at the point where money moves. Everything after the first small payment was conventional: contact on WhatsApp, pressure to pay more, remote access to the victim's computer under the guise of assistance, borrowed funds, and transfers to accounts controlled by criminals. Police described the operation as complex and significant, which places the video as one component of a longer chain rather than the whole of it.

Catching it would have required verifying independently who the victim was dealing with and confirming that the provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, which is the check the police pointed to. The identity of the figure in the video has not been made public, and no finding has been reported against any person named in connection with similar scams. That the video was AI generated is a police account of the case, and no arrest, charge or verdict is established in the reporting.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 in an investment scam, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The victim saw what appeared to be an AI generated video of a well known financial sector figure promoting an investment with claimed large returns. Police did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett.

After a small first payment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more. The fraudsters persuaded them to open several online accounts and gave themselves remote access to the victim's computer, saying they were helping with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and the funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. Police described the scam as complex and significant. Superintendent Joanne Gibson of the Scamwise Partnership urged people to pause and verify financial activity and for families to talk about fraud. Police advised checking independently who people are dealing with and confirming that providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
